sections.title: Three more owners
sections.content: You already know *-m*, *-d* and *-a / -e, -ja / -je* for 'my', 'your' and 'his/her'. Now add three more owners: 'our' is *-nk*, 'your' when you speak to several people is *-tok / -tek*, and 'their' is *-uk / -ük*.

sections.title: Linking vowel
sections.content: After a consonant, *-nk* and *-tok / -tek* need a linking vowel first, and it follows vowel harmony: *barát* → *barátunk*, *barátotok*. Remember *szobád* is 'your room' for one person; *szobátok* is 'your room' for several.

sections.title: Their: which ending?
sections.content: 'Their' follows the 3rd person singular ('his/her'). A word that takes *-ja / -je* for 'his/her' takes *-juk / -jük* for 'their': *szobája* → *szobájuk*, *barátja* → *barátjuk*.
A word that takes *-a / -e* for 'his/her' takes *-uk / -ük* for 'their': *kulcsa* → *kulcsuk*, *könyve* → *könyvük*.

sections.title: A few words change their vowel
sections.content: *szoba* lengthens its last vowel in all three forms: *szobánk*, *szobátok*, *szobájuk*. *név* does the opposite and shortens: *nevünk*, *nevetek*, *nevük* (not *névünk*). Learn such words one by one.

Only the ending changes the owner: *barátunk* is our friend, *barátjuk* is their friend — the rest of the word stays the same. *szobád* (one person) and *szobátok* (several people) are both 'your room' in English, but Hungarian uses a different ending for each.
